title: Each act, a blessing (Berakhot 60b)
hookLine: each morning blessing matches an action: opening eyes, stretching, standing
tomorrow: Akiva loses his lamp, his rooster, his donkey. what does he say?

lines: EVERY MOVE HAS A SENTENCE WAITING.
cards: Your watch buzzes: time to stand. Your phone counts your steps. A lot of tech now wants credit for noticing that you moved.
The Talmud has its own version, with no screen at all. It's still dark. Somewhere a rooster calls.
A person is lying in bed, eyes shut, not quite awake. And on one page of Berakhot, every small thing this person is about to do already has a sentence waiting for it. The eyes are about to open.

teach.h: THE ROOSTER, THE EYES, THE STRETCH.
teach.b: Here's the scene the Talmud walks through, in plain words. The rooster calls: blessed is the One who gave the rooster understanding, to tell day from night.
The eyes open: blessed is the One who opens the eyes of the blind. The person sits up and stretches: who releases the bound. Gets dressed: who clothes the naked.
Stands up straight: who raises the bowed down. Feet touch the floor: who spreads the earth over the waters. First steps: who makes firm a person's steps.
It's a morning told one movement at a time, and each movement gets its own thank you. Notice what kind of thank you. Not for the big things you planned.
For the things you'd never mention: eyes that work, a spine that straightens, ground that holds.

teach.h: NAMED BY WHAT YOU'D BE WITHOUT.
teach.b: Each line takes an ordinary act and names what it would be like without it: blind, bound, bowed. So waking up stops being automatic.
It becomes a list of rescues.

teach.h: FROM THE BEDROOM TO THE PRAYER BOOK.
teach.b: Today these blessings open the morning service in the prayer book, Birkhot HaShachar, and many people say them together there. But on this page they began in the bedroom, matched to the body, act by act.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the blessing for standing up is called zokef kefufim, the One who straightens the bent.
Someone recovering from an injury, practicing how to stand again, says the same words as everyone else, and may mean them more.

how: The morning blessings (Birkhot HaShachar) open the weekday morning service in the siddur; many say them aloud in synagogue or at home, and some say each one with its action, as Berakhot 60b describes.

o: one long blessing said once over the whole day ahead
the morning blessings: one for each thing the body does

s: the morning blessings started as a script for the synagogue only
on this page of Berakhot, each one is matched to a moment of waking up.
each blessing names what you'd be without the act: blind, bound, bowed
that's what turns an ordinary morning into a list of rescues.

games.q: your cousin just got her driver's license and says the first drive alone felt huge, then by day three it felt like nothing. what would Berakhot 60b suggest?
o: name what it would be like without it, so the ordinary act stays a gift.
save blessings for the first time; after that, it's just driving.
say one blessing a week for everything, so it doesn't get repetitive.
games.why: the morning blessings thank God for acts done every single day, each named by its opposite: blind, bound, bowed. repetition is the point.

practice: Sit in a chair, then stand up slowly, feeling your back straighten. As you rise, say the Talmud's words out loud, or your own: blessed is the One who raises the bowed down. Sit again, and stand once more, a little slower.

wordCard.voice: Each act. The morning blessings of Berakhot: one sentence for each thing the body does, from the rooster's call to the first step.

orig.note: Hebrew: who straightens the bent. the blessing for standing up.

carryVoice: Keep this one: each act, a blessing. Forty of fifty, and the book is nearly done.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 60b (the blessings on waking, each matched to its act: rooster, opening eyes, sitting up, dressing, standing, stepping on the ground, walking)
